subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 32-year-old man has had 4 months of low back pain and morning stiffness lasting more than an hour. The stiffness improves with exercise. He has tenderness at the Achilles tendon insertion and intermittent sausage-like swelling of the second right toe. Rheumatoid factor is negative.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this group of disorders?

options.text: They are strongly associated with rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP positivity
They are rheumatoid factor negative and HLA-B27 associated, sharing inflammatory back pain, enthesitis, and dactylitis
They are caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in the joint
They are type III hypersensitivity disorders linked to early complement deficiency
They are defined by anti-SS-A and anti-SS-B antibodies and exocrine gland destruction

explanation_correct: Seronegative spondyloarthritides are arthritides without rheumatoid factor and have a strong association with HLA-B27, a MHC class I serotype. The PAIR subtypes share variable features of inflammatory back pain with morning stiffness that improves with exercise, peripheral arthritis, enthesitis at tendon insertion sites such as the Achilles, dactylitis or sausage fingers, and uveitis. This patient's presentation is classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Rheumatoid factor positivity defines the seropositive group; seronegative spondyloarthritis is specifically rheumatoid factor negative.
explanation_incorrect.C: Monosodium urate crystal deposition causes gout, producing needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals, not a seronegative spondyloarthritis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Type III hypersensitivity with early complement deficiency underlies systemic lupus erythematosus, not these HLA-B27-associated arthritides.
explanation_incorrect.E: Anti-SS-A and anti-SS-B antibodies with exocrine destruction characterize Sjogren syndrome, not spondyloarthritis.

educationalObjective: Seronegative spondyloarthritis is rheumatoid factor negative and HLA-B27 associated, with inflammatory back pain, enthesitis, dactylitis, and uveitis.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 45-year-old woman with plaque psoriasis on her scalp and extensor surfaces notes pitting and yellow discoloration of her nails. She develops asymmetric swelling of several fingers, including a sausage-like digit, and pain in a distal interphalangeal joint. Radiographs show a pencil-in-cup deformity.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ankylosing spondylitis
Reactive arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis
Psoriatic arthritis
Osteoarthritis

explanation_correct: Psoriatic arthritis is associated with skin psoriasis and nail lesions and shows asymmetric, patchy joint involvement. Dactylitis and a pencil-in-cup deformity of the distal interphalangeal joints on radiograph are characteristic. It develops in fewer than one third of patients with psoriasis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ankylosing spondylitis causes symmetric involvement of the spine and sacroiliac joints with bamboo spine and aortic regurgitation, not asymmetric DIP disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: Reactive arthritis follows an infection and presents with conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis plus keratoderma blennorrhagica, not nail psoriasis and pencil-in-cup deformity.
explanation_incorrect.C: Rheumatoid arthritis is symmetric and erosive, rheumatoid factor positive, and lacks psoriatic nail lesions and pencil-in-cup changes.
explanation_incorrect.E: Osteoarthritis has Heberden and Bouchard nodes and degenerative changes rather than dactylitis and psoriatic nail disease.

educationalObjective: Asymmetric arthritis with dactylitis, nail lesions, and pencil-in-cup DIP deformity in a patient with psoriasis indicates psoriatic arthritis.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Pathology: Seronegative spondyloarthritis

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 26-year-old man has had progressive low back pain and stiffness for 2 years, worse in the morning and improved with activity. He has limited spinal mobility and tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, and he recently had an episode of acute anterior uveitis. Radiographs show sacroiliac fusion and a bamboo spine.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ankylosing spondylitis
Psoriatic arthritis
Reactive arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis

explanation_correct: Ankylosing spondylitis causes symmetric involvement of the spine and sacroiliac joints leading to ankylosis and a bamboo spine on radiograph. It is associated with uveitis, aortic regurgitation, and restrictive lung disease, is more common in males, and usually begins between ages 20 and 40. Inflammatory back pain that improves with exercise is characteristic.

explanation_incorrect.B: Psoriatic arthritis is asymmetric with skin and nail lesions and pencil-in-cup deformity rather than symmetric sacroiliac fusion and bamboo spine.
explanation_incorrect.C: Reactive arthritis presents with the conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis triad after an infection, not chronic symmetric spinal ankylosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Rheumatoid arthritis is rheumatoid factor positive with symmetric erosive peripheral small-joint disease and does not produce a bamboo spine.
explanation_incorrect.E: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis causes flowing ossification along the anterolateral spine but is not associated with HLA-B27, sacroiliac fusion, or uveitis.

educationalObjective: Symmetric sacroiliac and spinal ankylosis with a bamboo spine, uveitis, and inflammatory back pain in a young man indicates ankylosing spondylitis.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Pathology: Seronegative spondyloarthritis

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 38-year-old man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis develops progressive dyspnea on exertion. Pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity. His chest radiograph shows no interstitial infiltrates or effusion.
question: Which of the following best explains his pulmonary dysfunction?

options.text: Uveitis-associated inflammatory involvement of the lung parenchyma
Aortic regurgitation producing chronic pulmonary edema
Costovertebral and costosternal ankylosis restricting chest wall expansion
Apical fibrotic changes from a prior granulomatous infection
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage from immune complex deposition

explanation_correct: In ankylosing spondylitis, costovertebral and costosternal ankylosis can restrict chest wall expansion and produce restrictive lung disease. This explains a restrictive ventilatory defect with reduced total lung capacity in the absence of any parenchymal, vascular, or pleural abnormality on imaging.

explanation_incorrect.A: Uveitis is inflammation of the eye and does not cause pulmonary restriction or lung parenchymal disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: Aortic regurgitation can cause dyspnea from heart failure but would produce cardiac findings and pulmonary vascular congestion, not an isolated restrictive chest wall pattern.
explanation_incorrect.D: Prior tuberculosis with apical fibrosis would produce visible fibrotic changes on chest radiograph and apical findings, which are absent here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage causes infiltrates, hypoxemia, and hemoptysis rather than a chronic restrictive defect with a clear radiograph.

educationalObjective: Restrictive lung disease in ankylosing spondylitis results from costovertebral and costosternal ankylosis that limits chest wall expansion.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Pathology: Seronegative spondyloarthritis

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 28-year-old man is treated for bloody diarrhea due to a presumed bacterial gastroenteritis. Two weeks later he develops conjunctivitis, dysuria, and arthritis of the right knee. He also has hyperkeratotic skin lesions on his palms and soles.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ankylosing spondylitis
Psoriatic arthritis
Gonococcal arthritis
Gout
Reactive arthritis

explanation_correct: Reactive arthritis presents with the classic triad of conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis, summarized as can't see, can't pee, can't bend my knee. It follows infections with Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Chlamydia, or Yersinia and is associated with hyperkeratotic palm and sole lesions called keratoderma blennorrhagica. The preceding diarrhea and triad make this the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ankylosing spondylitis causes chronic inflammatory back pain and spinal ankylosis rather than an acute post-dysentery triad of conjunctivitis and urethritis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Psoriatic arthritis is associated with chronic plaque psoriasis and nail pitting, not a post-infectious triad with keratoderma blennorrhagica.
explanation_incorrect.C: Gonococcal arthritis in disseminated infection features tenosynovitis and pustular dermatitis, not the conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis triad after diarrhea.
explanation_incorrect.D: Gout causes acute monoarthritis with needle-shaped negatively birefringent urate crystals and lacks conjunctivitis, urethritis, and a diarrheal trigger.

educationalObjective: Conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis after a gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, with keratoderma blennorrhagica, define reactive arthritis.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Pathology: Seronegative spondyloarthritis

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 35-year-old woman with Crohn disease develops inflammatory low back pain and morning stiffness that improves with exercise. She has no skin psoriasis, no urethritis, and no recent diarrhea. Radiographs show sacroiliitis.
question: Which of the following best characterizes her condition?

options.text: It is strongly associated with rheumatoid factor positivity
It is a seronegative spondyloarthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease
It is caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition
It is a manifestation of SLE with early complement deficiency
It is caused by anti-SS-A antibodies

explanation_correct: Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis are often associated with spondyloarthritis. This is a seronegative, HLA-B27-associated disorder within the PAIR group, presenting with inflammatory back pain and sacroiliitis. The absence of psoriasis, urethritis, and a diarrheal infectious trigger supports the inflammatory bowel diseaseassociated subtype.

explanation_incorrect.A: Spondyloarthritides are by definition rheumatoid factor negative, so rheumatoid factor positivity would argue against this diagnosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Monosodium urate deposition causes gout, which produces crystal-positive monoarthritis rather than inflammatory back pain and sacroiliitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Systemic lupus erythematosus with early complement deficiency is a type III hypersensitivity disease with malar rash and serositis, not isolated inflammatory back pain in Crohn disease.
explanation_incorrect.E: Anti-SS-A antibodies are associated with Sjogren syndrome and neonatal lupus, not with inflammatory bowel diseaseassociated spondyloarthritis.

educationalObjective: Inflammatory back pain and sacroiliitis in a patient with Crohn disease represent a seronegative, HLA-B27-associated enteric spondyloarthritis.
